explanation: Fires on word-internal subword pieces in the middle of long, often technical or medical compound words (transga-str-ic, Intracere-bro-vascular, supra-cl-avicular, gastro-cnemius, phenylalanine hydro-xylase, SPI-R-IT) and on fragments of identifiers or names. The trigger is a non-initial or early piece of a word that is being spelled out over several tokens. There are scattered other hits (code indentation, 'per', 'of' in 'Battle of'), and ordinary whole words are weak.

Fires at clause or phrase boundaries where a continuation is expected: commas after a complete clause ('size, which'), the opening bracket or brace of a list or JSON object after a colon or '=', and closers of fixed idioms ('to be exact', 'full stop', 'at the moment', 'depending', 'in addition'). The context matters most: the token closes one unit and something new is about to follow. Content words in mid-phrase are weak.

Fires mostly on the subject or helper word in requests for help in Q&A text ('Can someone/anybody explain/help', 'if I may be so bold', 'I am using'). It also fires on the space before an age after a name ('Brittany Peoples, 20'), on 'of' in Wikipedia category lines ('Olympic shooters of Finland'), and on some fixed phrases ('by his own admission', 'request for comment'). These look like several unrelated jobs.

Fires on tokens inside conventional fixed expressions and set phrases, where the token is highly predictable from what came before ('bake for', 'known by locals as', 'STATE of Wyoming' in case captions, 'in the eyes of', 'alternating current (AC)', 'Democratic-Farmer-Labor', 'built-in', 'non-patent document'). The examples are mixed and share no clear lexical theme.

Fires on whitespace or layout tokens in documents with heavy fixed-width formatting: long runs of spaces, multiple newlines and the end punctuation of a line inside court-opinion captions (circuit headers, case numbers, judge signature blocks) and boxed license header comments in source code. Context matters: the token has to be padding or a line break inside a column-aligned, typeset-looking header. Ordinary prose whitespace does not fire.

Fires on short connector or operator tokens that join two values or items, above all the dimension 'x' between numbers (8 x 10, 18x24, 4x4) and 'versus'. Weaker hits come from license combiners ('v2.0 with', 'LGPLv3+', 'and later'), '+/-', the '**' exponent, timezone '+' and 'extends'. The token has to sit between two operands.

A mixture of contexts. It fires on the first token after an escape backslash in shell or LaTeX code ('\033', '\0', '\dfrac', '\pm'), on the first segment after 'package' or 'import' in Java ('org', 'com'), on 'games' in 'video games', and on miscellaneous others ('Supreme Court', 'std::cerr <<').

Fires on a capitalized or camelCase proper-name or identifier token that names a specific entity, typically right after a dot or a function-word slot: API or class names in code (RequestMethod, .jetbrains, HttpNotFound, .getBoundingClientRect, NSMutableDictionary, rootReducer), and named organizations or people in prose (NATO, Reuters, Kaepernick, Lenovo, LGPL). Activation is strongest for well-known framework or library identifiers.

No consistent trigger: it fires on varied tokens such as Go ':=' in test tables, 'data' in phrases like 'data volumes' or 'serial data', the prefix 'ant(i)', prepositions after a noun ('quality of life of', 'logger for', 'anger in'), and commas in lists. No shared token or context explains most examples.

Fires on the token right after a subject or a defined term, where the definition or value starts: '=' or '=x' in assignments and math definitions ('df=pd', 'F(n)=', 'G = (V,E)', 'Y_n ='), and verbs or adverbs that bring in a definition or description ('which mean', 'defined as', 'formerly known', 'commonly abbreviated', 'is basically', 'composed of'). Context matters: the subject is just being equated with or characterized as something.

Fires on the word 'business' (any case, incl. 'Business', 'BUSINESS', '_business') in nearly every sense: business days, business model, business interruption in licenses, business news. Strongest in compounds where 'business' modifies a following noun. Unrelated words are near zero.

Fires on the 'public' keyword (or the opening '{' after a namespace) that starts the main class or interface declaration right after the package/import or namespace header of a Java or C# file. Context matters: it needs the header-to-declaration boundary. Other hits elsewhere are weak and scattered.

Fires on a verb or plural noun right after a subject noun phrase, especially third-person present verbs that look like nouns ('capabilities lists', 'the other displays', 'coyote spots', 'chromosome pairs', 'the step signals', 'colour ranges', 'design changes'). The model seems to be resolving whether the token is the main verb after a subject. Words outside that subject-verb slot are weak.

A mixture. It fires on opening quotation marks that start a scare-quoted or coined term ('a "real" laptop', 'the "friends"'), on subword pieces in Scandinavian or Dutch words (skjer, vindt, helt, gjøre), and on pieces of citation IDs ('ijerph', 'ehp'). The quote-mark job is the biggest; the others look unrelated.
